article_title: ChatGPT improves creative problem-solving performance in university students: An experimental study
citation: Urban, M., Děchtěrenko, F., Lukavský, J., Hrabalová, V., Svacha, F., Brom, C., & Urban, K. (2024). ChatGPT Improves Creative Problem-Solving Performance in University Students: An Experimental Study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105031
title: Hybrid human-AI regulation (HHAIR) theory as applied to metacognitive demands of ChatGPT-assisted problem-solving
description: Hybrid human-AI regulation theory (attributed to Molenaar) holds that working with generative AI demands strong metacognitive skills because learners combine their own ideas with AI output: they must "select relevant information, reiterating and clarifying ideas, debugging errors, and adjusting their approach to ensure coherence and meaningfulness." The study uses the theory to motivate hypotheses about self-efficacy, monitoring accuracy, metacognitive experiences, and mental effort when solving ill-defined tasks with ChatGPT, and concludes that effective regulation requires students to attend to valid metacognitive cues rather than perceived ease.
requirements: Learners must possess or develop metacognitive monitoring and self-evaluation skills to assess AI-generated and self-generated ideas
Students must perform accurate self-evaluation of final outcomes containing both student- and ChatGPT-generated ideas
constraints: The study reports that perceived ease and usefulness act as invalid cues, so regulation based on metacognitive experiences alone may be inaccurate
target_learners: university students using generative AI tools
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring and self-evaluation of AI-assisted work
examples: The preregistered experiment measured self-efficacy, self-evaluation bias, task interest, difficulty, and mental effort with and without ChatGPT during a Product Improvement Task
key_sources: Urban, M., Děchtěrenko, F., Lukavský, J., Hrabalová, V., Svacha, F., Brom, C., & Urban, K. (2024). ChatGPT Improves Creative Problem-Solving Performance in University Students: An Experimental Study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105031

article_title: Scenario-based simulation training for the WHO hand hygiene self-assessment framework.
citation: Tartari E, Fankhauser C, Peters A, Sithole BL, Timurkaynak F, Masson-Roy S, Allegranzi B, Pires D, Pittet D. (2019). Scenario-based simulation training for the WHO hand hygiene self-assessment framework. Antimicrobial Resistance and Infection Control. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13756-019-0511-9
title: Three case scenario-based simulations for HHSAF completion training
description: WHO and the WHO Collaborating Centre developed an educational video, a promotional video and "three case scenario-based simulations (Tables 1, 2 and 3) for IPC specialists to simulate and fully assimilate the correct completion of the HHSAF framework in a standardized format". The scenarios depict a tertiary care centre (scored Advanced, 377.5/500), a rural Ugandan teaching hospital (Inadequate, 80/500) and a national referral hospital (Basic, 120/500), spanning a range of contexts and resource levels including low-resource settings.
requirements: Use by professionals in charge of implementing a hand hygiene improvement strategy
Use prior to completing and submitting data for the WHO global survey
constraints: Designed for simulation training purposes to achieve standardization and interactive learning
target_learning_goals: correct standardized completion of the HHSAF
examples: Case Scenario 1 (Bellevue University Medical Centre) scored 377.5/500; Case Scenario 2 (St. Mary's Teaching Hospital, Uganda) scored 80/500; Case Scenario 3 (Ulwazi National Referral Hospital) scored 120/500
key_sources: Tartari E, Fankhauser C, Peters A, Sithole BL, Timurkaynak F, Masson-Roy S, Allegranzi B, Pires D, Pittet D. (2019). Scenario-based simulation training for the WHO hand hygiene self-assessment framework. Antimicrobial Resistance and Infection Control. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13756-019-0511-9

article_title: The communication skills course for second year medical students at Hannover Medical School: An evaluation study based on students' self-assessments.
citation: von Lengerke Thomas, Kursch Angelika, Lange Karin, APG-Lehrteam MHH. (2011). The communication skills course for second year medical students at Hannover Medical School: An evaluation study based on students' self-assessments. GMS Zeitschrift für Medizinische Ausbildung 28(4), Doc54. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3244738/
title: 28-hour second-year doctor-patient communication course (HannibaL, MHH) with simulated patients, role play and OSCE-aligned observation sheets
description: A 28-hour, seven-session doctor-patient communication course in the second year of the HannibaL curriculum at Hannover Medical School, taught in groups of ten students. Its learning objectives are 'basic skills in taking patient histories, disclosing diagnoses (breaking bad news), and the use of shared decision-making (SDM) in these contexts', assessed at two of six OSCE stations; simulated patients join three of the seven sessions.
requirements: Small groups of ten students to allow repeated role play within the group and with the simulated patients
A pool of about 80 trained simulated patients and observation sheets combining the Calgary-Cambridge Guides criteria with those of Füeßl and Middeke
constraints: The article notes that implementing practice-oriented teaching in small groups using SP 'requires significant personnel, organisational and financial resources'
examples: In the 2009/10 academic year, 285 students took the course; two SP per group of ten enabled up to eight role plays per course group in the fourth session, and predefined cases covered diabetes mellitus type 2, hypertension, coronary heart disease and other OSCE-relevant diseases.
key_sources: von Lengerke Thomas, Kursch Angelika, Lange Karin, APG-Lehrteam MHH. (2011). The communication skills course for second year medical students at Hannover Medical School: An evaluation study based on students' self-assessments. GMS Zeitschrift für Medizinische Ausbildung 28(4), Doc54. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3244738/

article_title: Project-Based Learning in Introductory Quantum Computing Courses: A Case Study on Quantum Algorithms for Medical Imaging
citation: Nischal Binod Gautam, Keith Evan Schubert, and Enrique P. Blair. (2025). Project-Based Learning in Introductory Quantum Computing Courses: A Case Study on Quantum Algorithms for Medical Imaging. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.21321
title: The HHL algorithm as a three-subroutine quantum linear-system solver
description: The article describes the Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd algorithm as a quantum method for solving linear systems Ax = b with theoretically exponential speedup under ideal conditions. It structures HHL as "three main quantum subroutines": Quantum Phase Estimation encodes eigenvalues of A into a clock register, a controlled rotation encodes inverse eigenvalues into an ancilla qubit, and inverse QPE with post-selection yields a state proportional to the solution vector. The article uses this structure as the core technical content students implement in Qiskit.
requirements: The coefficient matrix A must be sparse, Hermitian, and well-conditioned for HHL to apply as described
constraints: Success of the controlled-rotation step depends on measuring the ancilla in the |1⟩ state, so post-selection limits output
Retrieving a specific solution entry generally requires repeated executions, reducing the exponential advantage
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students in introductory quantum computing courses
target_learning_goals: understanding quantum algorithm subroutines such as QPE and controlled rotations
critically evaluating classical versus quantum solvers
examples: Students implemented HHL in Qiskit with one ancilla qubit, five clock qubits, and two system qubits for the four-pixel vector
key_sources: Nischal Binod Gautam, Keith Evan Schubert, and Enrique P. Blair. (2025). Project-Based Learning in Introductory Quantum Computing Courses: A Case Study on Quantum Algorithms for Medical Imaging. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.21321

article_title: Integrity situational judgement test for medical school selection: judging 'what to do' versus 'what not to do'.
citation: de Leng W E, Stegers-Jager K M, Born M Ph, Themmen A P N. (2018). Integrity situational judgement test for medical school selection: judging 'what to do' versus 'what not to do'. Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5901405/
title: Deductive SJT development guided by two theoretical models: honesty-humility (positively related to integrity) and cognitive distortions (negatively related)
description: The article's deductive development approach grounds SJT response options in two established theoretical models. The honesty-humility (HH) subscale of the HEXACO personality inventory, which "has been demonstrated to be positively related to integrity", generated desirable responses, while cognitive distortions (CDs), "inaccurate thinking styles which may lead to antisocial behaviours", generated undesirable responses. Response options were assembled into seven categories across three HH facets (sincerity, fairness, modesty) and four CD categories (self-centredness, blaming others, minimising, assuming the worst).
requirements: Response options must be written to represent the HH facets and CD categories, aligning wording and reasoning within each category
constraints: The article notes the assumption that HH facets reflect good responses and CDs bad responses may be too simplistic, e.g. an HH-based response might entail betraying a friend
target_learning_goals: assessment of integrity as a non-cognitive attribute in medical school selection
examples: The Integrity SJT used 57 scenarios each with four response options: two HH-based and two CD-based, e.g. a cheating scenario with options representing minimising, modesty, self-centredness and fairness
key_sources: de Leng W E, Stegers-Jager K M, Born M Ph, Themmen A P N. (2018). Integrity situational judgement test for medical school selection: judging 'what to do' versus 'what not to do'. Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5901405/

article_title: Step-by-Step HHL Algorithm Walkthrough to Enhance the Understanding of Critical Quantum Computing Concepts
citation: Anika Zaman, Hector Jose Morrell, Hiu Yung Wong. (2022). A Step-by-Step HHL Algorithm Walkthrough to Enhance Understanding of Critical Quantum Computing Concepts. IEEE Access, Volume 3, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.09004
title: Step-by-step HHL walkthrough with 4-qubit bra-ket numerical example
description: A self-contained instructional artifact that explains the Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd algorithm analytically and mirrors each step with a 4-qubit numerical example in bra-ket notation, tracing all qubits without simplification. As the abstract states, "The HHL algorithm is explained analytically followed by a 4-qubit numerical example in bra-ket notation." The walkthrough covers the five HHL components: state preparation, quantum phase estimation, ancilla bit rotation, inverse quantum phase estimation, and measurement, with an Appendix reviewing basic concepts using examples from the main text.
requirements: Readers are assumed to have background in basis transformation, bra-ket and matrix representations, superposition, entanglement, encoding, controlled operations, measurement, quantum Fourier transformation, and quantum programming
constraints: The matrix A in the linear system problem is assumed Hermitian; non-Hermitian cases require conversion or more advanced treatment
target_learners: students learning quantum computing after basic concepts, potentially without a quantum mechanics background
target_learning_goals: understanding qubit evolution and interplay of basis transformation, superposition, entanglement, controlled operations, measurement, QFT, QPE, and quantum programming in a realistic algorithm
examples: The numerical example solves A = [[1,-1/3],[-1/3,1]], b = (0,1), giving x = (3/8, 9/8) with amplitude ratio 1:9
key_sources: Anika Zaman, Hector Jose Morrell, Hiu Yung Wong. (2022). A Step-by-Step HHL Algorithm Walkthrough to Enhance Understanding of Critical Quantum Computing Concepts. IEEE Access, Volume 3, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.09004

article_title: Step-by-Step HHL Algorithm Walkthrough to Enhance the Understanding of Critical Quantum Computing Concepts
citation: Anika Zaman, Hector Jose Morrell, Hiu Yung Wong. (2022). A Step-by-Step HHL Algorithm Walkthrough to Enhance Understanding of Critical Quantum Computing Concepts. IEEE Access, Volume 3, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.09004
title: Matlab code and qiskit circuit for the HHL numerical example
description: Two released code artifacts accompany the walkthrough: Matlab code implementing the numerical example from a pure matrix point of view, letting students trace how the wavefunction evolves rather than only seeing coefficient magnitudes as in IBM-Q, and a qiskit circuit that can be simulated and run on IBM quantum hardware. The article states "Matlab code corresponding to the numerical example is available for students to gain a deeper understanding of the HHL algorithm from a pure matrix point of view." Both are available at the referenced GitHub repository.
requirements: Access to Matlab and to the IBM-Q / qiskit platform for simulation and hardware execution
constraints: Hardware execution results are degraded by imperfection and noise in real quantum computers
target_learners: students studying the HHL algorithm from a matrix or programming perspective
target_learning_goals: tracing wavefunction evolution and understanding the HHL algorithm from matrix and circuit viewpoints
examples: The Matlab code prints the full 16-component Ψ9 state vector; the qiskit circuit runs on machine ibmq_santiago
key_sources: Anika Zaman, Hector Jose Morrell, Hiu Yung Wong. (2022). A Step-by-Step HHL Algorithm Walkthrough to Enhance Understanding of Critical Quantum Computing Concepts. IEEE Access, Volume 3, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.09004

article_title: Step-by-Step HHL Algorithm Walkthrough to Enhance the Understanding of Critical Quantum Computing Concepts
citation: Anika Zaman, Hector Jose Morrell, Hiu Yung Wong. (2022). A Step-by-Step HHL Algorithm Walkthrough to Enhance Understanding of Critical Quantum Computing Concepts. IEEE Access, Volume 3, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.09004
title: Five design characteristics of a complex-algorithm teaching example
description: The article enumerates the characteristics that distinguish its HHL teaching example from examples available elsewhere: a step-by-step, self-contained analytical discussion; a numerical example in bra-ket notation mirroring the analytical equations; Matlab code matching the numerical example exactly; qiskit code runnable in IBM simulation and hardware; and tracing all four qubits throughout without simplification. The article writes, "Firstly, the HHL algorithm is discussed analytically step-by-step and is self-contained. Secondly, a numerical example is given in bra-ket notation mirroring the analytical equations."
requirements: Availability of both matrix-based code and a programmable quantum circuit corresponding to the same example
constraints: Existing simpler examples often lack matrix representation and combine fewer core concepts
target_learners: students reinforcing basic quantum computing concepts with a relatively complex algorithm
target_learning_goals: appreciating the roles and interplay of basic quantum concepts in a realistic algorithm
examples: The paper's own HHL example exhibits all five characteristics, including tracing all 4 qubits without simplification
key_sources: Anika Zaman, Hector Jose Morrell, Hiu Yung Wong. (2022). A Step-by-Step HHL Algorithm Walkthrough to Enhance Understanding of Critical Quantum Computing Concepts. IEEE Access, Volume 3, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.09004
